title: Newlyweds and Accepting Influence
text:
In the late 1980s and early 1990s, John Gottman and his colleagues at the University of Washington in Seattle invited 130 newlywed couples into their laboratory. Each couple was asked to discuss an ongoing disagreement in their marriage for about fifteen minutes while the researchers videotaped them and coded every expression and remark. The couples were then followed for six years.

The researchers expected to find that the happiest couples practiced active listening, the technique often taught in therapy, in which one partner paraphrases and validates the other's complaint. Instead, they found that it was rare among all couples, happy or not.

What did predict divorce was a pattern of escalating negativity. Marriages were in more danger when discussions began harshly, when negative remarks were met with even stronger negative remarks, and when couples failed to calm things down with humor or affection. One finding drew particular attention: husbands who refused to accept influence from their wives, answering a complaint by escalating rather than taking any part of it on board, were more likely to end up divorced.

In stable, happy couples, conflict still happened. But it was softened, and both partners let the other shape their decisions.
lesson: In any close relationship, let the other person change your mind sometimes. How a disagreement starts and whether you calm it down matter more than perfect listening technique.
people: John Gottman, James Coan, Sybil Carrere, Catherine Swanson
source: Gottman, J. M., Coan, J., Carrere, S., and Swanson, C. (1998). Predicting marital happiness and stability from newlywed interactions. Journal of Marriage and the Family, 60(1), 5-22.
caveat: Some statisticians have criticized Gottman's divorce predictions as fitted after the fact to the same sample rather than tested on new couples.
